A new text classifier named fastText delivers high accuracy while running many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation [P2_p1_c02]. 

Traditional text classification often uses simple linear models, but they can struggle when dealing with large output spaces where some classes have very few examples [P2_p4_c02]. Common solutions use complex multilayer neural networks or factorize classifiers into low rank matrices [P2_p1_c04]. 

To solve this, the authors introduce fastText, which represents sentences using a bag of words and adds a bag of n-grams to capture partial information about local word order [P2_p1_c04][P2_p2_c03]. 

The results are striking. We can train fastText on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multicore CPU [P2_p1_c02]. It can also classify half a million sentences among 312K classes in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02]. On sentiment analysis tasks, its accuracy is often on par with deep learning classifiers and slightly better than some existing methods [P2_p1_c02][P2_p3_c02]. 

This matters because it provides a simple and efficient baseline that matches deep learning accuracy while drastically reducing the time needed to train and evaluate large text datasets [P2_p1_c02].
